articles.title_orig: AirPods Pro 3 vs AirPods 5: Three reasons to go Pro
articles.title_zh: AirPods Pro 3 vs AirPods 5: Three reasons to go Pro
articles.content_orig:
Apple debuted the all-new AirPods 5 this month, and they bring ANC to lower prices than ever before. If you’re shopping for AirPods, however, there are still several reasons you might want to opt for the more expensive AirPods Pro 3.
AirPods are one of Apple’s most personal products. The fit can vary dramatically between different people depending on the size of their ears. AirPods 5 offer an open-ear design, so they rest on the inside of your ear. AirPods Pro, meanwhile, offer a more traditional in-ear design with ear tips.
Personally, I find AirPods Pro to be more comfortable than AirPods 5. They’re also more secure for me, so I’m less worried they’ll fall out of my ears.
One of the key differentiators between AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods 5 is that AirPods Pro 3 offer built-in heart rate monitoring capabilities. During a workout, AirPods Pro can measure your heart rate to provide additional fitness metrics.
If you wear an Apple Watch, AirPods Pro 3 work along with your Apple Watch to ensure you get the most accurate data possible. Apple’s algorithms monitor the data from AirPods Pro and Apple Watch, and factor in the type of workout you’re doing, to use the most consistent data possible. For example, if you’re lifting weights and the Apple Watch ends up at an awkward angle on your wrist, AirPods Pro 3 will step in to provide more accurate data.
Furthermore, in iOS 27, Apple brought GymKit to the iPhone, so you can use iPhone and AirPods to get an Apple Watch-style experience … but without wearing a watch. Learn more about this change in Zac’s full coverage .
AirPods Pro 3 offer a range of hearing health features that aren’t available on AirPods 5. This includes:
With the Hearing Test feature, you can take a 5-minute test to identify if you have hearing loss. Apple’s Hearing Aid feature, meanwhile, is a clinical-grade hearing aid that uses the results of your test to craft a sound profile for your needs. Finally, Hearing Protection, can help prevent exposure to loud environmental noise.
There are other reasons to choose AirPods Pro over AirPods 5, including longer battery life, even better ANC, and a more capable charging case. The difference in ANC, in particular, is notable: Apple says AirPods Pro 3 offer 3x more Active Noise Cancellation than AirPods 5.

The designer statistic is the NFLâs silent assassin. Seemingly every outlier performance, both good and bad, is accompanied by a computer-generated information nugget that lets us know that teams in a similar position are a combined 987â1 when leading by three touchdowns in late September, when the temperature crests 72Â°, and the crescent moon hangs over the meadow. The songbirds sing of loversâ past, with your idiot team being the only one that has lost in that situation. I never know what to do when I see those, and also is anyone else with a supercomputer fact-checking these? Iâm not saying the computer is wrong, but it would be pretty easy for me to drop a stat like this into the ether, and everyone else would be like, Yeah, that sounds right. Â
Anyway, this one is infinitely more verifiable but similarly useless. I donât know what to do with the information that Klint Kubiak is the first head coach to begin the season 3â0 after his team had the No. 1 pick the previous season since Vince Lombardi. Similarly, I donât know what to do with the information that the previous two Raiders coaches to start their first season 3â0 were John Madden, who went to the AFC title game in that 1969 season, and Bill Callahan, when the Raiders made it to the Super Bowl in 2002.Â
Which is why I think a post on assessing the âsurpriseâ teams through three weeks of the 2026 season is due. We can snack on AI-generated tidbits all we want about Kubiak and the Raiders, but we should dive into the circumstances by which this came to be a surprise and, through that exploration, decide whether it matters all that much. Along with the Raiders, weâll get into a few other teams in similar circumstances, though they wonât all be 3â0.
Iâm going to rate each team by the highly scientific ârealnessâ rating. These teams are either âextremely real,â âpretty darn real,â âa perfectly normal amount of real,â ânot all that real,â orâgaspâânot real at all.â Indeed, people who read this article all the way to the end boast a 68.7% chance of experiencing a moment of immense personal joy.Â
Realness: Pretty darn realÂ
Why: Hereâs a wild statistic about the Raiders that I think matters. The Raidersâ defense has forced eight fumbles and recovered one. That kind of luck differential doesnât seem to matter for a team that is maximizing its drives better than almost any other team in the NFL. Through three weeks, the Raiders have punted only 12 times, with a handful of those coming in garbage time. The Raiders have also scored on two of their three scripted drives at the beginning of the game. Las Vegas is one of the 10 teams most likely to end its drive in a touchdown so far this year, and while weâre still operating with an incredibly small sample size and one of the Raidersâ wins was against the Dolphins, a team that overwhelmingly has the highest odds to attain the No. 1 pick in 2027, what we saw on Sunday against a more formidable Saints team looks to be the Raiders weâll be getting for a majority of the year.Â
In Sundayâs win, the Raiders became a 12-personnel team (one running back, two tight ends). That isnât all that surprising given that Brock Bowers returned and, if two of your five best offensive players are tight ends, youâll want them on the field together. But the Raiders won a game (Week 1) in which they were a majority 21-personnel team (a two-back, typically fullback-oriented offense) and a Week 2 game in which they were primarily an 11-personnel team (one running back, one tight end and three wideouts). Now that Bowers is on the field, and he played primarily as a wide receiver against the Saints, it gives the Raiders a kind of peak-49ers-like versatility that makes the team very difficult to prepare for. At the very least, we now know the Raiders arenât going to be run over. Having come into the week with the leagueâs best pass-block win rate, Kirk Cousins will remain relatively comfortable in the pocket and, all of a sudden, projecting six wins out of the teamâs remaining schedule (without any real upsets) doesnât seem ridiculous whatsoever. The Raiders still have games with the Titans, Cardinals, Jets, Browns and the limping Patriots, and, oh by the way, the calling card of a true Kubiak tree offenseâthe ground gameâhasnât even found its footing yet.Â
Defensively, the Raiders remind me of the 2025 Bearsâ offense in that theyâre enjoying health and peak performance from a handful of newly imported free agents. The Raidersâ remake of their linebacking corps has been nothing short of transformative.Â
Realness: A perfectly normal amount of real
Why: The Steelers are 2â1, and while we cannot in the same breath celebrate the Raidersâ win over the Dolphins and completely discount a narrow Steelers victory over the Falcons in the opener, we can point out two very different circumstances in those games. Pittsburgh, for one, needed a miraculous defensive play to edge a really bad Cooper Rushâled Falcons team. The Steelers deserve immense credit for dressing down a Bengals defense that came into this game in the top five in sacks, touchdowns allowed, passing touchdowns allowed, yards per game allowed and turnovers created. But we saw what is still possibleâand the defining upsideâof the Aaron RodgersâMike McCarthyâera Steelers: creating embarrassing coverage busts against the Bengals. The Cincinnati secondary was on ice skates, though Iâm almost certain Rodgers will never have pocket time like this again. Rodgers averaged a season-high 3.19 snap-to-throw time Sunday, and Jaylen Warren gouged the Bengals for 7.5 yards per carry. That allowed Rodgers to be more effective in play-action, which the Steelers used on more than 20% of his dropbacks for a 1.14 EPA per play. To McCarthyâs credit specifically, some of the concepts heâs been playing withâlike a Rams-ian, Seahawks-ian Ben Skowronek insert concept that created an open touchdownâshows that the old ball coach can still dig into his bag and dial up some impressive shots.Â
DK Metcalf appearing to get over whatever was bothering him over the first two weeks of the seasonâPittsburgh had lost the most EPA per play to drops in the NFL to that pointâis also a major upgrade.Â
The debut of Max Iheanachor was encouraging, with the rookie offensive tackle allowing the lowest pressure percentage of any of Pittsburghâs offensive linemen on Sunday. If Iheanachor turns into a great drop-back anchor tackle, I may increase my optimism levels because giving the most arm-talented quarterback of his generation light-years of time in the pocket is a sound strategy if itâs replicable.Â Â
Iâm a little more muted in my praise at the moment because I want to see what a very old Steelers team looks like on short rest against a division rival in a suddenly-hostile environment (weâll get to that Week 4 game against the Browns in a moment) and then a matchup against a Colts team that could test Pittsburghâs so-far mediocre run defense, which is allowing above a 40% success rate to opponents this season.Â
That should give us a better sense of whether the perceived strengths of this teamâagain, an offensive line that could be very, very good, and a pass rush that, so far, has a success rate about as high as the vaunted Vikingsâcan hold up over a long period of time.Â
Realness: Not all that real (yet)
Why: I need to, for a moment, separate two things. The young core of this roster is potentially great. Mason Graham showed as much on Sunday in a win over the Panthers in which he was virtually unblockable. He registered seven pressures and two sacks, equally as masterful in the stunt game as he was against double teams. We can continue to go on and on about how Harold Fannin Jr., Austin Barber, Spencer Fano and Denzel Boston are making the leap, and we should. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg are among the tech executives expected at a Tuesday luncheon with President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, CNBC confirmed, according to multiple people familiar with the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the details are not public.
Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai will also be at the lunch, the company confirmed Monday, as well as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to MS Now. OpenAI President Greg Brockman will be in attendance as well, Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other administration officials are hosting an all-day event on Tuesday to announce a new website for federal information and resources, according to a White House official. That event will have panel discussions on artificial intelligence , energy, space and other topics.
Anthropic co-founder and Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown will also be in attendance at the event, according to a person familiar with the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the details are not public.
Last week, multiple big tech executives attended the state dinner for the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping, including Apple's Tim Cook, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su.
Amodei, who was notably absent from Thursday's China state dinner, had a private dinner with the president on Sunday. It was the first one-on-one meeting between the two leaders, according to a person familiar with the visit, who asked not to be named in order to discuss a confidential matter.
Tuesday's meeting could serve as another opportunity for tech leaders, particularly Amodei, to ease tensions with the White House as the debate over AI safety has spread and leaders have taken sides on potential regulation. A former Anthropic researcher triggered the outcry after he accused AI frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."
Industry leaders like OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Musk have agreed with calls for an industry-wide slowdown, after Amodei penned an essay calling for companies to "pace the frontier" with advanced AI. articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Nolo was on the verge of becoming a major Category 5 storm early Monday as it moved farther away from Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center said. It was expected to continue gaining strength, reaching peak intensity on Monday before gradually weakening.
The storm is forecast to remain well south and southwest of Hawaii's main islands but approach the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument on Tuesday. That's a vast, 582,000-square-mile protected conservation area northwest of Hawaii.
Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 155 mph early Monday, making it a Category 4 storm. Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 35 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 150 miles.
Nolo was forecast to bring up to 20 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island. For Maui, 4 to 8 inches were possible. The rest of Hawaii was likely to get 1 to 3 inches, with 5 at most, enough to trigger isolated flooding, forecasters said.
What's more, Nola-generated swells "will be affecting south-facing shores of the main Hawaiian Islands for the next few days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions," the hurricane center cautioned early Monday.
All state parks on Hawaii's Big Island and on Maui were closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.
President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said.
Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo , continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.
The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.
Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

articles.title_orig: Arming an adversary: Why Trump’s offer to sell China weapons belies US policy
articles.title_zh: Arming an adversary: Why Trump’s offer to sell China weapons belies US policy
articles.content_orig:
In an offer that baffled most observers, United States President Donald Trump has made a pitch to his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping that has seldom been made in modern history.
Trump’s suggestion that Beijing buy US weapons was another off-script remark that appeared to stray from official policy, prompting the State Department to clarify that Washington has no such plans.
Trump asked Xi “at one point” whether China was interested in procuring US arms, the US envoy to Beijing, David Perdue, said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday. The president reportedly made the suggestion in discussions with Xi about US arms sales to Taiwan , but it was unclear whether that happened during their joint summit last week or at another time.
The comments are all the more striking given Washington’s concerns about Beijing’s support for Iran, as Trump’s ongoing war with Tehran continues.
Analysts were quick to dismiss Trump’s proposal as lacking any strategic logic – not least of all due to the arms embargo the US has imposed on China since 1989.
“Such ‘gambits’ by Donald Trump [are] spontaneous flights of fancy that are not part of any strategy,” Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong, told Al Jazeera.
“It is certainly unusual to suggest to your main strategic rival and adversary [that it] should buy your weapons.”
But experts also said it revealed how Trump views Beijing: through a strictly mercenary framework.
The analysts were in agreement that Trump’s offer was not a serious proposal and possibly even a joke.
US law strictly prohibits arms sales to China and Washington officially identifies Beijing as its primary strategic and economic competitor – so there is no practical policy framework for such a transaction, said Beijing-based analyst Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation.
“It is an off-the-cuff negotiating probe designed to disrupt standard diplomatic scripts, test reactions and create transactional leverage,” Tangen told Al Jazeera.
The US has always viewed China and its military capabilities with concern, citing its Communist Party’s fusion with the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as a threat. It has accused Beijing of acquiring and diverting the world’s cutting-edge technologies – including through theft – in order to achieve “military dominance”, a US State Department memo states.
“The US officially regards China as a leading national security threat,” said Reyes.
“The Pentagon’s long-term military planning treats China as the ‘sole pacing threat’, meaning that the US military reckons its technological edge, naval capacity and now its AI progress primarily against China’s capabilities and performance.”
Trump’s remarks were therefore a departure from the policy underpinnings of his administration – and that of previous administrations.
“The remark highlights the friction between Trump’s transactional political style and a national security establishment that views China as a systemic rival to be contained,” said Tangen.
Trump’s motivation, he explained, is based on his need to acquire rare earth metals to replenish America’s depleted weapons stockpiles – which have taken a major hit following his ongoing war with Iran. China dominates the world’s rare earth supply chains.
William Yang, a senior analyst on North East Asia at Crisis Group, agreed that Trump views Beijing through a transactional lens – and that his offer held no realistic, strategic thinking.
“This incident reflects Trump’s almost pure transactional view of Washington’s relationship with Beijing,” Yang told Al Jazeera. It’s also in line with the president’s conduct throughout his second term – making remarks that contradict existing US policies, which sow confusion and require clarification later, he added.
History offers few examples of geopolitical rivals striking arms deals, making Trump’s proposal particularly unusual. Yet, there are a handful of precedents.
During World War II, the US’ Lend-Lease Act to Allied countries also included the Soviet Union – as they were driven by a common enemy, Nazi Germany, explained Tangen.
Years later, technological cooperation between the US and China in the late Cold War “was motivated by a shared objective of countering Soviet power and it never involved frontline technology”, he said.
Dov H. Levin, a professor of international relations at the University of Hong Kong, also pointed to the Iran-Contra affair, when in the eighties, the US sent secret weapons transactions to Iran and Nicaragua – which violated the US Congress and the stated public policy of the government at the time.
“I see no US weapon system that the US would plausibly offer China to purchase in the current state of their bilateral relationship,” Levin told Al Jazeera.
Britain sold jet engines to the Soviet Union in 1947 during the early Cold War, said Reyes. Nazi Germany, in turn, sold the Soviet Union an unfinished heavy cruiser in 1940, during their temporary rapprochement, before invading the country the following year, he added.
“These cases show how commercial or strategic interests have sometimes permitted military transactions between countries that were rivals or subsequently became adversaries,” said Reyes.
But Tangen argued that such transactions reflected “temporary alignments born of immediate geopolitical necessity”.
The analysts agreed that the historical examples do not translate to the relationship between China and the US today.
“What distinguishes today’s China-US relationship is that the two countries are directly competing over the strategic balance of power in the Asia Pacific and beyond – and are even said to be heading for inevitable kinetic conflict,” said Reyes.
If Trump genuinely wanted to use US weapons as a bargaining chip with Beijing, there are multiple barriers in his way, not least of all national security constraints, said the analysts.
Selling weapons to Beijing “would potentially compromise US national security, allow China to gain access to advanced US defence technology and further bolster China’s military modernisation efforts,” said Yang.
Additionally, US systems do not align with Beijing’s security architecture, said Tangen.
“The US model is built for global power projection. Platforms like the F-35 combine extreme technological sophistication – such as stealth, sensor fusion and electronic warfare – but depend on an expensive, vulnerable ecosystem of tankers, AWACS, satellites, forward bases and global logistics,” Tangen said.
The Chinese model, meanwhile, is built for regional defence and sovereignty protection, he added.
“Systems like the J-20 [Chinese fighter jet] are integrated into a robust regional framework combining long-range missiles, drones, domestic sensors, satellites and land-based command-and-control, all backed by a massive industrial base capable of high-volume mass production,” said Tangen.
Reyes was blunt in his analysis of Beijing’s need for US arms: “China now produces most of its own weapons. Why would it need to buy American?”
With the two powers gridlocked in competition over AI , rare-earth metals, the question of Taiwan and the Iran war – their race to increase military exports is no exception.
While Trump may have made the weapons proposal to bolster US arms exports, China has no interest in helping a country that sees it as an existential threat, said the analysts.
The US continues to dominate global arms exports, but China is edging its way higher, becoming the world’s fourth biggest exporter, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Beijing has largely turned to niche markets in the Global South.
“China has carved out a market for affordable drones, combat aircraft and conventional weapons, particularly in Pakistan [and other parts of] Asia, Africa and the Middle East,” said Reyes.

articles.title_orig: Prosecutors are reexamining a Cornell fraternity rape case. Here's what we know
articles.title_zh: Prosecutors are reexamining a Cornell fraternity rape case. Here's what we know
articles.content_orig:
People walk on the campus of Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., in 2024. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
New York prosecutors say they are reopening an investigation into an alleged rape case from 2024 that involved Cornell University students.
This comes after the alleged victim, referred to as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court of the State of New York this month. In it, she claims multiple men drugged and brutally raped her for more than four hours at a Cornell fraternity house in October 2024.
In a nine-page statement, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten announced efforts are underway to reexamine the case. Once his office determines appropriate charges, the case will be presented to a grand jury, he said. Van Houten said he has assigned a senior prosecutor, with experience in sex crimes, to start preparations.
Cornell University issued a statement following news that prosecutors are taking another look at the case.
The school said it supports the decision but defended how university officials handled the case two years ago. Kyle Kimball, vice president for university relations at Cornell, said the school "conducted a thorough Title IX investigation" that lasted several months.
No criminal charges were ever filed.
But Cornell said it held a hearing where "a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days," which included testimony from all sides.
At the end of that hearing, expulsions and suspensions were issued. The statement did not specify which individuals faced those consequences.
Kimball continued in the statement: "Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false."
The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity, of which the alleged rapists were members, was banned from the campus two years ago, when details first emerged.
Doe is suing seven alleged rapists, the fraternity, Cornell University and others.
Her attorneys didn't respond to a request for comment before publication.
The case became subject to fierce social media scrutiny following Doe's lawsuit. Van Houten said people have called his office to demand answers as to why the case was never investigated. Others called to insult and threaten, he said.
Van Houten acknowledged the outrage. In defending his office, he said the civil lawsuit's claims differ from the unnamed victim's sworn statement from two years ago.
"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," he wrote. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."
Van Houten added that his office had never been contacted by Doe's attorneys.
"Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision," he said. Van Houten said he reached out to Doe's attorneys to understand "the discrepancy."

President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023 , but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday , citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN , showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third , which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said : “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem , who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán . “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters .
Rep. Thomas Massie , a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter , congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “ public service announcements .” A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act , the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure .)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

articles.title_orig: Sixers’ LeBron James, ‘living in the moment,’ squashes retirement talk
articles.title_zh: Sixers’ LeBron James, ‘living in the moment,’ squashes retirement talk
articles.content_orig:
A little after noon on a dreary Monday morning, kids wearing school uniforms spilled onto the playground in downtown Camden.
It was recess at LEAP Academy, and the kids milled about the macadam or waited their turn on the swings, contentedly unaware that, just a few blocks away, the King had just arrived to claim his new kingdom.
At around 11:15 a.m. ET, LeBron James followed a phalanx of front office and public relations staff into a second-floor room, sat down behind a table draped in blue cloth and promptly began clearing the table. He took a water bottle meant for his sipping and plopped it on the floor, yanked a microphone off its stand and finally glanced at a placard with his name.
“You guys know who I am, right?” he said, before putting the name card on the floor, too.
This, of course, is why James is here, wearing the red, white and blue of the Philadelphia 76ers: To rearrange things. To bring structure and order to a franchise that has been mired in mediocrity.
And, if all goes as he plans, to upend the NBA pecking order.
“I didn’t leave my family,” he said of his relocation to Philly while his family stays encamped out west, “to lose in the second round.”
Had the Liberty Bell still been able, it might have peeled off in glee at that moment.
In his first official duty as a 76er, James hit all the proper notes. He spoke graciously for nearly 20 minutes, waxing thoughtfully about the difficulty of juggling parenthood with superstardom, and sharing honestly his reasoning behind joining the Sixers. He invoked the Palestra (he played there as a high schooler) and paid proper homage to the demanding fan base (“We respect you, but we hate you. I love that,” he said).
But it is those 11 words that Philly fans, who are at 25 years and counting without so much as a berth in the Eastern Conference Finals, will devour. The question, of course, is whether they will be on James’ statue or carved into his gravestone.
Declarations here – of independence and otherwise – have a way of hanging around. The same people who embraced Moses Malone’s prediction of “Fo Fo Fo,” about the Sixers’ 1983 NBA title run (it wound up Fo, Fi, Fo) also remember that, 31 years ago, Ricky Watters replied, “For who? For what?” when asked why he didn’t lay out for a throw from quarterback Randall Cunningham.
“They know sports. They know ball,” James said of his new fan base. “But if you’re not doing what you’re supposed to do, they’re going to let you hear it. They’re going to hold you accountable.”
The worry about what will come, though, is for another day. For once, the September Sixers offered excitement about what could be.
Ordinarily the Sixers’ media day would have fallen largely on deaf ears, a speed bump on a calendar filled with far more important dates. Nine hours after the Sixers commenced their interviews, the undefeated Eagles would play the Bears on “Monday Night Football.” On Tuesday, when training camp officially begins in Camden, the Phillies begin their quest for “Red October,” after belatedly securing a wildcard slot in the eleventh hour.
But this Saturday, the Sixers will play their Blue x White scrimmage in the downtown arena for the first time, to allow for more fans, and the get-in price for the home opener is already pushing toward $300. Actual media day, usually reserved for a few ink-stained regulars, was near standing-room only, with one team official bemoaning a Phoebe Bridgers concert that prevented the team from moving the event to the team’s home arena in Philadelphia.
This is what hope looks like, what it feels like when a franchise actually has a plan and not just a process. General manager Mike Gansey pulled off the coups of the offseason, not just signing James but securing Jaylen Brown in a trade with the Celtics that was as brazen as it was stealthy.
“If it had leaked,” executive vice president for basketball operations Jameer Nelson told CNN Sports. “I’m not sure it happens. That’s just my opinion.”
Brown’s arrival started the ball rolling. Tyrese Maxey sealed the deal. The precocious 25-year-old became a workout pal with James post-Covid 19 pandemic, the two bonding on their insatiable desire to do the work. In the offseasons since the pandemic, they became regular partners, both hitting 6 a.m. workouts together. Clearly impressed with Maxey’s dedication and pluck, James asked him for an honest evaluation of the Sixers.
Still – even though Philly was on James’ agent’s famed whiteboard of destinations – it seemed like a long shot even to those involved.
VJ Edgecombe was getting a pedicure when he heard about his new teammate and Nelson was at an AirBnB in Huntington Beach, California, for his daughter’s softball tournament when the news became official. Unable to tell his family, Nelson played dumb until Jayce started screaming, “LeBron is coming to Philly!”
Once the deal was done, Edgecombe set about creating a new team text chain.
“But I don’t have LeBron’s number,” he said with a grin. “And even I did, I wasn’t adding him to it. I made Tyrese do that.”
Even those on the text chain admit they’re still a little starry eyed. James officially became a Sixer on July 27, but this is his first time in Philly (that he arrived on the heels of a Nor’easter reminded him of what he’s in for with the East Coast weather).
“I thought I was over it,” Jabari Walker said. “But then it was like, ‘Wait. He’s in the locker room now.’”
On Tuesday, James will be on the practice court. That is, frankly, where he plans to do his best work. He can still play – “the luxury of my game is I can do everything,” he quipped. “Literally I can do everything” – but he thrives in creating an incubator for success. He threw shade at unnamed players who averaged big numbers in their careers, but secured no postseason success, and pooh-poohed an “instant oatmeal” society that wants everything handed out easily.
James loves, at the risk of using a word that will make Philly fans flinch, “the process,” but his comes with four championship rings on his fingers.
“You have to fall in love with doing things that are uncomfortable,” he said. “And if we can do that, we can be a great team. If we don’t do that, then we’ll be like, ‘Oh man. That was a great team on paper and we had a lot of great talent, and we lost in the second round.’”

articles.content_orig:
Week 3 was all about the nail-biter.
Of Sunday’s 14 games, 12 ended within one score, and most came down to the final play, including Matthew Stafford 's last-second interception to cement the Rams' second-half collapse at Denver in the nightcap.
Let’s run through key storylines in the aftermath of a Sunday that provided a plethora of heart palpitations, including:
But first, we head to Brazil, which hosted an early contender for Game of the Season on Sunday.
Football’s ability to inspire never ceases.
Ravens kicker Tyler Loop rode a rocky path during his rookie campaign, culminating in a season-ending miss in the team’s Week 18 loss to the rival Steelers with the AFC North title (and the accompanying playoff berth) on the line. That pushed 44-yard kick attempt set in motion an offseason of change in Baltimore. Loop fended off questions about his future, keeping his job despite the immense fallout.
A blocked attempt in Week 2’s disappointing loss to the Saints revived questions about the 2025 draft pick. Then, on Sunday in Rio de Janeiro, Loop got his shot to brush away the haze of the past.
After the Ravens' defense bowed up and kept Dallas out of the end zone late in the fourth quarter, seven seconds remained in 31-31 game. Lamar Jackson rocketed a missile that Zay Flowers leaped to snag for a 27-yard gain , with the receiver immediately getting down as Jackson called a timeout with 1 second remaining and the ball now at Dallas' 38-yard line. Loop lined up the 56-yard attempt and calmly banged it through, with CBS Sports' Jim Nantz eloquently calling the game-winning boot “a trio in Rio.”
Ravens players celebrated with their sometimes-maligned kicker as they pulled off a last-second victory despite stumbles along the way.
Loop’s kick on Sunday didn’t erase the previous big miss or guarantee anything about his future. However, it provided oxygen to a flickering flame. That one kick could have revived a career.
"I was saying on the sideline, 'Your legacy starting now,' because I feel like he has been facing adversity," Jackson said of Loop . "I said, 'What a way to start your legacy in Brazil,' and he finished the rest. He did it. Shout out to special teams, shout out to Loop."
Jackson’s part shouldn’t be understated, either. His ability to deliver that late laser over the middle -- without taking too much time -- was pivotal, as was Flowers' snag and haste to get down. The Ravens moved the ball well on Sunday, but they also were stuffed in short-yardage situations several times.
In a young season in Jesse Minter’s first campaign, the 34-31 win showed fortitude: from the defense keeping the Cowboys out of the end zone on their final drive to Jackson making a play to Loop nailing the winner. It’s the type of victory that could propel a team.
The Ravens needed the win in a hotly contested division.
The Steelers' offense showed life in a 30-27 victory over the Bengals, with Aaron Rodgers finally hitting on some deep strikes after two weeks of them falling incomplete. If the Pittsburgh offense can keep splashing plays, and Rodgers isn’t broken in half, the Steelers will be a tough out.
Cincinnati’s defense came back to the pack a bit after an excellent start to the season. That’s not too much of a surprise. That’s not why Cincy lost, however. Special teams issues were the real killer, as the punt crew gave the Steelers extra chances. Joe Burrow still had a shot late, but a final-drive fumble sealed it. It’s a stinging loss to a division rival, but not one that should worry Bengals fans.
The Browns' defense was locked in again to improve Cleveland to 2-1 , stymying Bryce Young and a Panthers offense that had moved the ball well in the first two weeks. Deshaun Watson showed that, when he avoids the big mistake, he can be a net positive for Cleveland and make game-winning plays. That’s new.
The Patriots were pegged to regress in 2026, partly because of their tougher schedule after winning the AFC East. That might be one element of New England's 1-2 start, but it’s far from the story.
The biggest issue isn’t that the Pats are facing teams that make them pay for mistakes; it’s that Drake Maye has regressed to the point that he’s making rookie-level blunders in Year 3. Week 1’s calamitous turnover fest in Seattle has snowballed. Maye has seven giveaways through the first three games of the season, the most by any player in the NFL. His seven turnovers are the most by a Patriots player in the team's first three games of a season over the last 30 years, per NFL Research.
Perhaps he can explain away the embarrassing fumble in Sunday's blowout loss to Jacksonville, saying there was blood on the ball from the center. But there was no excuse for his second-quarter interception in the end zone. It was a ball that should never have been thrown. That’s Maye’s biggest issue right now: He’s not seeing things clearly. Defenses studied his weaknesses all offseason, and he hasn’t adjusted. Until Maye does, more upchucks like Sunday's performance will ensue.
"I think quarterbacks want to make plays,” Vrabel said Monday morning on the Greg Hill Show, via ESPN's Mike Reiss . “I think they want to throw touchdowns. I think sometimes when Greg and I go golfing, we really want to make a good score, right? Sometimes we’re so focused on it, we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways.
"We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in and go play football and not try to force things that aren’t there.”
Gregg Rosenthal, Jourdan Rodrigue and Nick Shook recap the Week 3 matchup between the Raiders and the Saints.
I already noted last week that the way Las Vegas has been winning is different under Klint Kubiak. It feels repeatable.
The defense has been opportunistic, taking advantage of turnovers. Las Vegas had four takeaways in the fourth quarter of its Week 3 win at New Orleans. The Raiders had only three fourth-quarter takeaways in the entire 2025 season, according to NFL Research. It’s also the first time a team has forced at least four fourth-quarter takeaways in a game since the Cowboys in Week 13 of 2022 vs. the Colts. Yes, the Raiders benefited from a controversial fumble call on Tyler Shough . It also takes players creating such opportunities to benefit from them.
Tight end Brock Bowers ’ return was pivotal. Vegas doesn’t win in NOLA without his 10-catch, 116-yard, one-TD performance. Kubiak deployed Bowers all over the formation, in-line and detached, making him a matchup nightmare. Despite Bowers missing the first two games after undergoing a knee procedure, a magical season for the TE appears quite viable, with Kirk Cousins force-feeding his top target. This offense needs one more outside option to be complete.
The Raiders are the darlings of the league right now, and rightfully so. Kubiak has quickly shown he can win in the big chair. His coordinators have been excellent. Cousins has been steady. Playmakers are making plays. But I should point out that the Raiders' opponents are a combined 1-8 through three weeks. The real test comes in next Sunday, when Kansas City visits Las Vegas .
“It’s a great f---ing win,” Raiders star defender Maxx Crosby said postgame in the locker room . "But we’ve got a great f---ing team coming into town. We already know what it is. It’s the f---ing Kansas City Chiefs.
“Enjoy this s--- tonight, take care of your bodies, and we’re f---ing on a warpath to get what we want, men.”
San Francisco 49ers fans should thank their stars for Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey -- and pray they don’t succumb to the injury bug that continues to plague the club.

State of play: President Trump has spent the past week lashing out at AI "doomers" and boiling the race down to a single imperative: beat China.
The other side: China is every bit as determined to win the AI race, but its leader Xi Jinping — who lands in Washington Wednesday for his first state visit since 2015 — is balancing two competing fears:
Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications.
Reality check: So far, nobody has publicly defined what would make the red phone ring.
Between the lines: Washington and Beijing already have crisis hotlines, as well as a history of going dark when they're needed most.
The bottom line: The very existence of the proposal is an acknowledgment that AI is no longer just another arena of U.S.-China competition. A serious failure on either side could quickly become a shared crisis.

Hello football friends, and welcome to the Monday edition of the Pick Six newsletter!
If you're still trying to recover from Sunday's NFL action, welcome to the club. Every time I thought Week 3 couldn't get any crazier, it somehow got crazier. In the early slate of games, we saw the Commanders -- who just LOST their starting quarterback last week -- take down the undefeated Super Bowl champion Seahawks 33-31.
That was one of seven upsets that we saw in Week 3.
If you felt like every game on Sunday was close, you're not crazy. There were a total of 12 games decided by a single possession, which is tied for the most for any day in NFL history and the most for any week in league history. If we get a one-score game tonight, that will set the NFL record for most one-score games in a week, but don't count on that happening, because every Monday night game has been a blowout so far.
Anyway, it's Monday, so you probably already know what's coming your way: We've got grades from every game, plus some overreactions. And of course, we'll be breaking down the J.J. MCCARTHY TRADE that went down on Monday afternoon.
As always, here's your daily reminder to tell all your friends to sign up for the newsletter. To get them signed up, just click here .
For the first time ever, CBS got to air an international game and it ended up being possibly the craziest international game of all time with the Ravens beating the Cowboys in Rio De Janeiro. Maybe the NFL should put all their games in Rio.
Next time there's a game in Rio, I'll be requesting to go, but I didn't go this time because I was way too busy handing out grades. I graded every game from Week 3 and here's a look at the grades from two notable games that were played Sunday:
Ravens 34-31 over Cowboys in Rio de Janeiro
Steelers 30-27 over Bengals
As for the other 26 grades that we handed out so far in Week 3, you can check those out by clicking here .
You can't have a week of NFL action without having winners and losers, so we have some winners and losers. Carter Bahns came up with this week's list, and we're going to check out his losers below. At the top of our losers' list is a QB who was in the Super Bowl just seven months ago.
If you want to see Carter's list of winners (and a couple of other losers), be sure to click here .
Everyone on the internet loves to overreact to things, and that's especially true when we're talking about the NFL. Personally, I overreact to everything. With that in mind, Zach Pereles decided to take a look at several things that happened during Week 3 to decide if we're all overreacting.
Statement: The Raiders are going to make the playoffs. Overreaction or reality: Overreaction. The Raiders can only play who is on their schedule, and their wins are now over the Chargers (who look miserable), the Dolphins (who might not win a game) and the Saints (who might be good but might be just OK).  Let me be perfectly clear: It's OK if the Raiders aren't going to make the playoffs. They already have as many wins this year as they did last year. Kubiak has done wonderful stuff, the young players look great, the free agent additions look great, and it's already one of the most impressive turnarounds of the year.
Statement: Trevor Lawrence is a dark horse MVP candidate. Overreaction or reality: Reality. Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes and could have ran for another score (he kneeled). The difficulty level on some of his throws is really impressive. Lawrence is simply playing at an extremely high level. He wasn't great last week at the Broncos , but as we've already seen, every quarterback has off weeks. He is finally unlocking everything we projected he could be when he was coming out of Clemson: big arm that can access the entire field, impressive athleticism and awesome downfield accuracy, especially over the middle of the field.
Statement: Brock Purdy is playing as well as he ever has. Overreaction or reality: Reality. Let's give Brock Purdy his due. This season, he ranks: 1st in net yards per attempt (9.5), 1st in EPA per dropback (0.62), 1st in success rate (65.6%), 1st in touchdown rate (10.8%), 3rd in completion percentage (72.3%). Now, Kyle Shanahan always has uber-efficient offenses. He's also doing this with no Ricky Pearsall , no De'Zhaun Stribling and no DeMarcus Robinson . Mike Evans left Sunday's game, too.

With that in mind, here are 10 crazy stats from Week 3:

The Bears and Eagles will try to end the drought tonight and it should be an interesting matchup. For one, the Bears won't have Caleb Williams . Wait, we're getting a backup QB going up against the 2-0 Eagles? Crap. Maybe this Monday night blowout trend is going to continue.

If you're thinking about betting on the game, here are a couple of props.
If you're wondering how my props are doing this year, I'm 5-5 (2-3 on kicker props and 3-2 on all other props).
And now, it's time for some picks.

That's right, we're all on the Eagles. If it makes Bears fans feel any better, we we're all on the Packers on Thursday night and that one definitely didn't work out for us.
Over on our CBSSports.com picks page , all seven of our seven experts are taking the Eagles to win and cover as a 3.5-point favorite.
It's been a busy few days around the NFL, and since it's nearly impossible to keep track of everything, I put together a quick roundup for you.

After Jaxson Dart got injured last week, John Harbaugh made it clear that the Giants were going to add a quarterback and that's exactly what they did on Monday by acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings.

Getting a fifth-round pick in return for a guy who was taken 10th overall isn't ideal, but it's better than nothing. As for the Giants, this a classic Harbaugh move. McCarthy played for Jim Harbaugh at Michigan and you can bet that John gave his brother a call before making the decision to go after McCarthy.
The Giants' offense is at its best when a mobile quarterback is running the show and New York just wasn't going to have that with Jameis Winston under center. articles.title_orig: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.title_zh: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to revive for now a Bureau of Prisons policy cutting off certain medical interventions and social accommodations for transgender inmates.
The Justice Department's emergency appeal stems from a federal district court order issued last month that continued to prohibit the Bureau of Prisons from enforcing its new rules against any inmate who is or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria.
The judge overseeing a challenge to the policy, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, ordered the Trump administration to continue providing medical care to a class of transgender inmates.
A group of inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria filed a lawsuit last year after President Trump issued an executive order at the start of his second term that prohibited the use of federal funds for medical procedures or treatments for transgender inmates within the federal Bureau of Prisons system. On the heels of that directive, the bureau issued new guidance that prohibited staff from granting requests for clothing accommodations for those inmates and barred the use of federal dollars for medical interventions.
The Bureau of Prisons then issued a new policy in February that it said was independent of Mr. Trump's executive order. Under those rules, the agency would continue providing mental health services for inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria, but would not provide surgeries, hormone therapy or social accommodations, like chest binders, wigs or breast padding, to address gender dysphoria.
Lamberth agreed to block the new rules in June and ordered the Bureau of Prisons to continue providing medical treatments to transgender inmates. The judge ruled in part that the administration's new policy was "reverse engineered" to implement Mr. Trump's executive order. He then issued an order last month continuing to block enforcement of the rules.
The Justice Department appealed. Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to restore the policy while proceedings moved forward.
In its request for emergency relief to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration accused the district court of "substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency." The Bureau of Prisons, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said, determined its policy on medical treatments for transgender inmates was "necessary to maintain institutional security," and he warned that the district court's decision "nullifies" that judgment.
Sauer said the lower court order "prevents the application of the Executive's chosen policy" on a broad basis.

Your T-Mobile bill is about to become more expensive even if your plan isn’t changing and you think you are a part of some sort of price lock. T-Mobile, once it stopped including fees within its plan prices, opened itself up to a world where they can increase prices at will through those same fees that you at one time never really gave thought to.
The T-Mobile “ Regulatory Programs & Telco Recovery Fee ” is increasing for the second time in 2026, this time by a larger $1.00 per month. This is actually the 3rd time in less than 2 years that this fee is going up.
The new Regulatory Programs & Telco Recovery Fee will increase to $5.49 per month per voice line after previously increasing in January 2026 from $3.99 to $4.49 per month . In April 2025, it also saw an increase from $3.49 to $3.99 . In 18 months, with no changes to your plan, your bill has gone up $2.00 per month for each line.
On T-Mobile’s fees & charges page , they updated the text this morning to note the price increase and its relatively immediate active date of October 12, 2026 . You have a couple of weeks left before your T-Mobile bill increases.
You can see there that mobile internet lines are also seeing a $0.50 per line increase each month as well, from $2.10 to $2.60.
We’ll try to remind you when October 12 rolls around and you head to the internet to ask, “Why is my T-Mobile bill more expensive this month?”

The 12-team fight to MLB's finish line and the World Series trophy that comes along with it starts now.
OK, maybe not now now, but with the regular season closed and the playoff field set, these franchsies know exactly what stands between them and championship glory.
While no one knows which organization will rise above and how the other 11 will get tripped up, multiple experts have shared their ideas. Let's break down some of those expert picks to get a feel for what might be coming to an MLB playoff environment near you.
Between Yahoo Sports and CBS Sports , there are full round-by-round predictions from nine different experts. Among the four Wild-Card Round matchups, there isn't universal agreement on any of them.
There is, however, one series that comes awfully close. Eight of the nine experts have the New York Yankees knocking off their longtime rival Boston Red Sox.
No other series had more than six experts agreeing on one side. The closest were the Atlanta Braves beating the Philadelphia Phillies, and the San Diego Padres ousting the Chicago Cubs, which both outcomes appearing on six of nine brackets. The biggest split came between the Chicago White Sox and Houston Astros with five favoring the former and four backing the latter.
Advancing a round didn't bring our first universal agreement among the experts. One came awfully close, though. ( And, yes, it is exactly what you're thinking .)
The two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers were projected Division Series winners by eight of the nine experts. The only dissenter, CBS Sports' Dayn Perry, backed the Braves.
Experts saw two other heavy favorites in the field. Both the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers were picked by seven of the nine experts. The Yankees snagged the other two picks on the AL side, while the Cubs and Padres drew one apiece in the NL.
The only team with a first-round bye that didn't receive overwhelming support was the Cleveland Guardians, which checks out when they were the only non-98-plus-game winner among the top two seeds (they won 85). Cleveland was predicted to escape this round by five experts, while four went with the resurgent White Sox, who followed three consecutive 100-loss seasons with an 84-win rise.
The closer these projections get to the finish line, the more the opinions split.
In the AL, the consensus opinion among the experts crowned the Rays, who drew six of the nine votes. That included four picks of them over the Guardians and two where they knocked off the White Sox. For the other outcomes, two had the Yankees defeating the Guardians, while one went Cleveland over Tampa Bay.
In the NL, it was the Brewers—not the Dodgers—receiving the most love. Six different experts had Milwaukee escaping the NL: three by beating L.A., two by eliminating San Diego and one by knocking off the Cubs. The Dodgers, meanwhile, were twice predicted NL winners (once over the Brewers, once over the Padres), while the Padres were the last predicted winner (over the Dodgers).
Now that we've made it this far, let's crown some (predicted) World Series champions, shall we?
The Brewers received the strongest backing with five of the nine experts going their way. The most popular World Series pick was Milwaukee over Tampa (four experts' opinons), while one more had Milwaukee defeating New York.
The Rays and Dodgers were the only other predicted winners, as they split the final four votes. Tampa's predicted wins came over San Diego and L.A., while L.A.'s were against Cleveland and New York.

articles.title_zh: Selloff in U.S., European Government Bonds Deepens
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Yields on the longer end of the curve rose further to multidecade highs on Monday as a bond sell-off deepened.
The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), often referred to as the most critical number in global finance for its widespread use as a benchmark rate, advanced roughly 5 basis points to 5.25%, its highest level since 2007, when yields rose in the run-up to the Great Financial Crisis.
Further out on the curve, 30-year Treasury yields ( ^TYX ) advanced by 6 basis points to 5.57%, a level not touched since 2004. The short end was also under pressure, as the 2-year yield ( 2YY=F ) rose by roughly 8 basis points to 4.93%.
Read more: How soaring Treasury yields could hit your finances
Bets on further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, an energy crisis kicked off by the war in Iran, ballooning US government debt and budget deficits, and a historic investment cycle driven by the AI build-out have all contributed to a sell-off that has spooked investors.
Of those concerns, the Federal Reserve is perhaps the biggest focus for investors. Earlier in September, the Fed issued a quarter-point rate hike, raising the US target lending rate for the first time in three years.
"We now have data broadly defined that says the economy has indeed strengthened," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press conference following the meeting. "Underlying growth is higher. Inflation is the problem. Stable prices have been the problem for now more than five and a half years."
More notable than the hike itself, however, were projections indicating that a majority of voting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) members expected at least another quarter-point hike, reinforcing a higher-for-longer outlook for rates. Four FOMC members saw the need for the Fed to hike rates by 50 basis points in 2026.
The FOMC's price stability mandate has pushed the Fed to raise rates, per Warsh's statement. The war in Iran has made that mandate more consequential as it pushes up energy prices around the globe, increasing strain on businesses and consumers.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
The AI boom has added another source of upward pressure.
A surge in spending on data centers, chips, power generation, and other infrastructure has helped keep US investment and economic growth resilient, even as financing costs have climbed. That strength can push yields higher by reducing the case for lower interest rates, while the enormous capital requirements of the build-out are adding to "competition for capital," or the demand for financing across the economy.
Taken together, those forces have driven investors to demand substantially higher yields on US government debt as they digest stronger growth, stickier inflation, expectations for tighter Fed policy, and a swelling supply of Treasurys needed to finance federal deficits. The result has been a sharp repricing across the curve.
Rising yields aren't necessarily bearish for growth, Macquarie global strategists Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry argue. Rising Treasury yields often represent economic growth — when investors expect stronger activity, firmer demand, and continued wage increases.
"The reason to worry about the recent rise in long-term yields, if there is any, is not because they will slow the economy," the strategists wrote. "That way of thinking inverts the truer causality: yields are high partly because the economy is strong and bond issuance is high. And the economy is strong mainly because of the AI-induced infrastructure investment cycle."
Problems arise, Wizman and Berry wrote to clients on Monday, when yields rise too quickly, as they largely have since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Rapidly rising yields can "fall disproportionately on one company, lender, or whole sector that had over-leveraged in the low-yield environment of 2021," the strategists wrote. Even if that outcome remains contained, concerns can still trigger volatility in the wider market.
Investors will be carefully watching this week's US PCE price-change report — the Fed's preferred measure of inflation — and Friday's September jobs report, both set to be key macro indicators for the FOMC's path forward.

articles.title_zh: Over 800 Killed in Renewed Houthi-Saudi War in Yemen, W.H.O. Says
articles.content_orig:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
I n the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.
As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”
He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.
Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west , seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.
The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen , with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.
The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.
Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.
He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.
“Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”
His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.
“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.
Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.
“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.
The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.
“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.
The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.
Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.
“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.
The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.
“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update.
After updating to version 1.0.981607934 of the Pixel Buds app, we’re seeing @Pixel Buds in Gemini as the latest Connected App. You can control “settings like EQ preset, ANC mode, conversation detection, and touch controls.”
This brings up the Gemini overlay, with a “Connecting to Pixel Buds” message appearing along with verbal confirmation.
On devices without the app update, those commands just open the system Bluetooth settings page.
We’re seeing Pixel Buds 1.0.981607934 widely rolled out via the Play Store today.
The three other features Google previewed presumably require a firmware update. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 will get Dynamic ANC that adjusts to “compensate when subtle shifts in the seal happen,” like if the buds move in your ear. There’s also Pixel Watch sleep sync that pauses music, disables touch controls, and silences notifications on the Pixel Buds. Finally, you will be able to trigger Live translate by tapping your Pixel Buds.

articles.title_zh: Vikings send J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick
articles.content_orig:
The Giants have added a new quarterback to the mix in the wake of Jaxson Dart’s season-ending injury .
Big Blue are acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round pick, according to multiple reports.
McCarthy, 23, was the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, four picks after the Giants selected wide receiver Malik Nabers.
Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.
After leading Michigan to a national championship, McCarthy missed his entire rookie season due to a torn meniscus, struggled in 10 starts last year and lost the starting job to Kyler Murray this year.
He had been Minnesota’s third-string QB, with Carson Wentz starting in place of an injured Murray in Week 2.
McCarthy was coached at Michigan by Giants head coach John Harbaugh’s brother Jim, and the two spoke about the quarterback before the trade, according to Fox Sports’ Jay Glazer.
Jameis Winston started for Dart in the Giants’ rain-soaked Week 3 win over the Titans at MetLife Stadium and went 14-for-22 with 118 yards with zero touchdowns and zero turnovers. He was sacked three times.
The 32-year-old, who was the No. 1 overall pick by the Buccaneers in 2015, signed a two-year, $13 million contract extension before the season, a sign that the Giants had confidence in his ability to keep the ship steady if Dart were to get injured.
But his ugly effort in relief of Dart during a Week 2 loss to the Rams was cause for concern.
The only other quarterback on the Giants’ roster was Jake Haener, a 27-year-old 2023 fourth-round pick who had 39 career pass attempts, all in 2024 with the Saints. He was elevated from the practice squad for Sunday’s game.

articles.title_orig: Next entry-level Kindle may get rounded screen corners and new colors
articles.title_zh: Next entry-level Kindle may get rounded screen corners and new colors
articles.content_orig:
Amazon may be preparing a new version of its entry-level Kindle. Leaked marketing images show an e-reader that resembles the 2024 model but has flatter edges, rounded display corners and a power button on its right side.
The images, shared by leaker Roland Quandt, show the device in several pastel colors. The Kindle name appears below the screen and on the back, but Amazon’s smile logo is absent from the images.
The power button is another visible change. Rather than sitting on the bottom edge, as it does on the current entry-level Kindle, it appears near the top of the new device’s right-hand side.
The leaked images seem to show two slightly different designs. In some, the screen appears nearly flush with the front of the reader and has a more pronounced border. In others, it looks more recessed. The sample text also differs in size and spacing.
Those differences do not confirm that Amazon intends to release two models. The images could depict separate variants, but they could also show preliminary designs or marketing materials that will change before launch.
Images of new cases for a Kids version have also surfaced. For now, Amazon has not announced the e-reader, and its specifications, price and release date remain unknown.

iPhone Duo is coming October 23 , but there are several unannounced features coming to its StandBy mode that were just discovered hidden in Apple code.
When iPhone Duo arrives next month, it will be the most versatile iPhone yet. That’s in part due to its two displays, but also thanks to special modes that are available in different setups.
You can use iPhone Duo folded or unfolded, in landscape or portrait, and in “seated” or “standing” configurations.
Standing is a great setup for watching videos, but it also enables a range of new StandBy features. And unlike previous iPhones, you can use iPhone Duo’s StandBy mode even when it’s not charging.
Apple showed off several StandBy examples at its unveiling earlier this month. But additional features have just been uncovered by leaker pdfu.
